topic: Law and privacy for AI on patient records in an NRW university hospital (status 22 Nov 2026)
summary: As of 22 November 2026 a German university hospital can reuse its own care data for research without individual consent under section 6 GDNG, but only with pseudonymisation, role control, logging, public information and in principle no transfer to third parties. The NRW health data protection act (GDSG NW) has been repealed since July 2025; section 17 DSG NRW is the general state-law basis for research. German regulators describe retrieval-based AI with source references, possibly on-premise, more favourably than training on records, which creates memorisation risk. The AI Act's high-risk duties were postponed to December 2027 and August 2028, and whether a summariser is a medical device is contested and depends on the intended purpose. Several reforms (GeDIG, MDR revision, GDPR omnibus) are still drafts; this is background and no legal advice.

findings.claim: Section 6 of the German Health Data Use Act (GDNG) lets a health care institution reuse its own lawfully stored care data for quality assurance, medical research and statistics without asking each patient for consent.
findings.detail: Conditions in the text: the reuse must be necessary, the data must be pseudonymised and later anonymised as soon as the purpose allows, there must be a roles-and-rights concept with logging, and the data must be deleted after 30 years at the latest. The public must be informed in plain language and patients can ask for details. It is a permission for the institution, not a private licence for a single researcher.
findings.quote: sind zu pseudonymisieren; sie sind zu anonymisieren, sobald dies im Rahmen der Weiterverarbeitung
findings.source: GDNG section 6, gesetze-im-internet.de
findings.talk_use: Q&A: the main legal door for research on the hospital's own records; always name the conditions with it.

findings.claim: Under section 6 GDNG personal data may in principle not be passed to third parties; joint use by publicly funded hospital networks needs, among other things, approval by the data protection authority.
findings.detail: Exceptions are consent, another legal basis, anonymised transfer, or joint processing by publicly funded associations of health institutions. For the last one the controller's interests must considerably outweigh the patients' interests; the authority should decide within one month.
findings.quote: Die Weitergabe der personenbezogenen Daten an Dritte ist im Rahmen der Weiterverarbeitung nach Absatz 1 untersagt.
findings.source: GDNG section 6(3), gesetze-im-internet.de
findings.talk_use: Q&A on multi-centre work such as RACOON: local processing is simpler than pooling; pooling needs its own basis.

findings.claim: The Bavarian data protection authority reads section 6 GDNG as covering the whole health care institution, not only the treating department; it says medical faculties, institutes and chairs are outside the institutions that may form a joint-use network.
findings.detail: Orientation guide of 1 January 2026, margin numbers 104 (whole institution, rejecting a narrower reading in the literature) and 129 (faculties not covered, stated for the network clause). Bodies outside can take part as processors under Art. 28 GDPR. Bavarian view only; no NRW guidance was found.
findings.quote: insbesondere solche aus dem Hochschulbereich (wie etwa medizinische Fakultäten, Institute und Lehrstühle), nicht davon umfasst
findings.source: Bayerischer Landesbeauftragter für den Datenschutz, Orientierungshilfe Datenschutz und GDNG, v1.0
findings.talk_use: Q&A for doctoral candidates: are you acting for the hospital or for a university institute? This changes the legal basis.

findings.claim: North Rhine-Westphalia repealed its Health Data Protection Act (GDSG NW) by a law of 10 June 2025, in force on 1 July 2025.
findings.detail: Article 15 repeals the act of 22 February 1994; Article 20 sets entry into force on the first day of the month after promulgation (27 June 2025). Many web pages still show the old act. Older NRW advice that cites GDSG NW is therefore outdated.
findings.source: GV. NRW. 2025 S. 530, Articles 15 and 20
findings.talk_use: Q&A: shows that even the rulebook changed recently; do not cite GDSG NW as current law.

findings.claim: Section 17 of the NRW Data Protection Act allows health data to be processed for scientific research without consent if this is necessary and the interests of the person do not prevail.
findings.detail: It requires protective measures and anonymisation as soon as the research purpose allows; identifying features must be stored separately until then. The act covers public bodies; a legal overview brochure from an NRW anonymisation project names university hospitals explicitly. How section 17 relates to section 6 GDNG for UKM was not found in any official guidance.
findings.quote: auch ohne Einwilligung für wissenschaftliche oder historische Forschungszwecke oder für statistische Zwecke zulässig
findings.source: DSG NRW section 17, version valid from 1 April 2026
findings.talk_use: Q&A: the state-law basis for university research, with a balancing test.

findings.claim: A federal bill (GeDIG) would replace the GDNG and state explicitly that own-data research includes developing AI models and AI systems in health care.
findings.detail: Bundestag printed paper 21/8279, draft section 24 replaces today's section 6. The explanation says this covers training, testing and validating. Bundesrat opinion 25 September 2026, committee hearing 14 October 2026. No evidence was found that the Bundestag has passed it by 22 November 2026. The state data protection authorities, commenting on the May draft, asked for clearer wording that it must always be research.
findings.quote: einschließlich zum Entwickeln von KI-Modellen und KI-Systemen
findings.source: Bundestag, Gesetzentwurf GeDIG, Drs. 21/8279
findings.talk_use: Q&A 'may we train on our data?': today arguable under research; a clarification is pending, not law.

findings.claim: In Westphalia-Lippe, doctors who take part in research using data that can be linked to a specific person must make sure an ethics committee is consulted beforehand.
findings.detail: Section 15(1) of the professional code, reworded by the 11th amendment (published 3 December 2025, in force the next day). A new paragraph 2 lets doctors notify their participation if colleagues were already advised. The duty is addressed to doctors. The wording does not settle how pseudonymised or fully anonymised retrospective data are treated, so ask the committee.
findings.quote: Körpermaterialien oder Daten verwendet werden, die sich einem bestimmten Menschen zuordnen lassen
findings.source: Ärztekammer Westfalen-Lippe, 11th amendment of the Berufsordnung, MB.NRW 2025 Nr. 184
findings.talk_use: Q&A: a legal basis for data use does not replace ethics advice; ask the Ethik-Kommission before starting.

findings.claim: German criminal law on medical secrecy (section 203 StGB) allows doctors to involve outside service providers only as far as this is necessary to use their service.
findings.detail: Making secrets available to one's own professional assistants and trainees is not disclosure. Outside contributors can be punished themselves for unlawful disclosure (paragraph 4), and failing to bind them to secrecy can be punishable. Secrecy applies in addition to the GDPR.
findings.number: up to 1 year prison or fine (para. 4)
findings.quote: soweit dies für die Inanspruchnahme der Tätigkeit der sonstigen mitwirkenden Personen erforderlich ist
findings.source: StGB section 203, gesetze-im-internet.de
findings.talk_use: Q&A: why pasting records into a private chatbot account is more than a data protection issue.

findings.claim: Health care providers may process health data in the cloud only under section 393 SGB V: data location limits, an establishment in Germany and a current C5 security attestation, since 1 July 2025 in principle of type 2.
findings.detail: Location: Germany, EU, equated states, or a third country with an EU adequacy decision. Systems new on the market after 30 June 2025 may use type 1 for the first 18 months; equivalent certificates can be recognised. Customer-side criteria must also be implemented. This is a security condition and does not supply a legal basis for a given research purpose (inference).
findings.quote: ein aktuelles C5-Testat der datenverarbeitenden Stelle im Hinblick auf die C5-Basiskriterien
findings.source: SGB V section 393, gesetze-im-internet.de
findings.talk_use: Q&A 'why not simply use a cloud LLM?': possible in principle, but with conditions; on-premise avoids this section, though not GDPR or secrecy.

findings.claim: The German data protection authorities state that a retrieval-based AI system (RAG) can process health data if the legal requirements are met, because the data stay in the reference documents and are not permanently stored in the language model.
findings.detail: Condition: no targeted training or fine-tuning on these data. The paper also says RAG can make on-premise operation possible and so avoid sending data to online providers. Every RAG system still needs its own legal basis, and a language model itself cannot control who may see what.
findings.quote: da diese nicht dauerhaft im LLM verbleiben, sofern kein gezieltes Training oder Nachtraining des LLM mit diesen Daten stattfindet
findings.source: Datenschutzkonferenz, Orientierungshilfe RAG, v1.0
findings.talk_use: Strong regulator support for 'retrieve and cite' instead of 'train on everything'.

findings.claim: The same authorities say that documenting the sources used for an answer makes the model's input traceable, but how the model turns it into an answer remains hard to explain.
findings.detail: They describe hallucinations as reduced, not eliminated, depending on document quality. They also warn of membership inference and data poisoning against the document store. Data subject rights in language models are called largely unsolved.
findings.quote: ermöglicht diese die Nachvollziehbarkeit und Transparenz des Inputs des LLMs
findings.source: Datenschutzkonferenz, Orientierungshilfe RAG, v1.0
findings.talk_use: Slide on the chain of proof: regulators value source references and say where they stop.

findings.claim: The EU Court of Justice ruled on 4 September 2025 that pseudonymised data are not automatically personal data for everyone, because a recipient may be unable to identify the person.
findings.detail: Case C-413/23 P, paragraph 86, on Regulation 2018/1725 for EU bodies. The duty to inform is judged from the controller's side at collection (paragraphs 111 to 115). For a hospital that keeps the key, its own pseudonymised records therefore remain personal data.
findings.quote: pseudonymised data must not be regarded as constituting, in all cases and for every person, personal data
findings.source: CJEU, EDPS v SRB, C-413/23 P
findings.talk_use: Q&A: 'it is pseudonymised, so GDPR does not apply' is wrong inside the hospital.

findings.claim: The Council agreed on 21 October 2026 to keep the GDPR definition of personal data and to add a new Article 25a on pseudonymised data; this is a negotiating position, not law.
findings.detail: Reported by a law firm on 9 November 2026; it also mentions a clearer definition of scientific research and draft EDPB Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation. Primary Council text not read.
findings.quote: would keep the GDPR definition of personal data but add a new Article 25a
findings.source: Lewis Silkin, Digital Rulebook: Simplification of EU data protection and cyber rules
findings.talk_use: Q&A outlook: the GDPR may change, but plan with today's law.

findings.claim: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 postponed the AI Act's high-risk duties to 2 December 2027 for listed uses (Annex III) and to 2 August 2028 for AI in regulated products (Annex I), which include medical devices.
findings.detail: Signed 8 July 2026, published 24 July 2026. In Annex I only machinery was moved out of Section A; medical devices stay there under this regulation. A recital clarifies that being integrated into a regulated product does not in itself mean that an AI system fulfils a safety function.
findings.quote: 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I
findings.source: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), Official Journal
findings.talk_use: Q&A on AI Act timing: correct any slide that still says August 2026 or 2027.

findings.claim: The AI literacy duty in Article 4 AI Act still exists but was softened in July 2026: organisations must take measures to support AI literacy and need not guarantee a level for each person.
findings.detail: Applies to providers and deployers for their staff and others who operate AI for them, in relation to context and affected persons.
findings.quote: This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.
findings.source: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, new Article 4 AI Act
findings.talk_use: Q&A: training staff on what LLMs can and cannot do is a legal duty, in softened form.

findings.claim: The AI Act does not apply to AI systems developed and put into service solely for scientific research, nor to research, testing and development before market launch or use.
findings.detail: Articles 2(6) and 2(8). Testing in real-world conditions is not covered by the second exemption. The exemption does not touch the GDPR, medical secrecy or ethics rules. Using a research tool for routine care would likely end the exemption (inference).
findings.quote: specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development
findings.source: AI Act (EU) 2024/1689 Article 2(6) and (8), text as shown on artificialintelligenceact.eu
findings.talk_use: Q&A: research use is lighter under the AI Act, but a switch to care changes the picture.

findings.claim: EU guidance says a simple record search is not a medical device, but search with natural language processing is no longer 'simple search' when it contributes to a medical purpose.
findings.detail: MDCG 2019-11 rev. 1, June 2025. Electronic records that only replace paper are not devices, while modules that analyse patient-specific data for a medical purpose can be. Guidance endorsed by the MDCG, not law. Word searches found no example of an LLM summariser in it.
findings.quote: software that performs search using Natural Language Processing (NLP) where those actions contribute to achieving a medical purpose
findings.source: MDCG 2019-11 rev. 1, Guidance on qualification and classification of software
findings.talk_use: Q&A: the line runs along the intended purpose, not along the technology.

findings.claim: Experts disagree whether LLM summarisers of patient records are medical devices under EU law.
findings.detail: A peer-reviewed law article (2025) suggests classing summarisation tools as devices because they take part in the diagnostic process, case by case. Regulation professor Stephen Gilbert told a trade magazine (about 2024, date not shown) that it can be argued either way and that an EU regulator would be unlikely to class them as devices; source https://insights.citeline.com/MT154472/AI-Clinical-Summarization-Tools-Sit-In-Regulatory-Grey-Area-Experts-Warn. No BfArM position was found.
findings.quote: this paper suggests classifying these systems as medical devices under the MDR
findings.source: Blatti, When Are LLMs for Clinical Documentation Considered Medical Devices Under the MDR?, BioLaw Journal 4/2025
findings.talk_use: Q&A: the honest answer is 'grey area', with named experts on both sides.

findings.claim: Hospitals may build and use their own medical devices under Article 5(5) MDR without most of the MDR's requirements, if a list of conditions is met.
findings.detail: Conditions include no transfer to another legal entity, a quality management system, a justification that no equivalent product on the market meets the need, a public declaration and review of clinical experience. The safety and performance requirements of Annex I still apply. Transfer to network partners is the critical point for shared tools.
findings.quote: the devices are not transferred to another legal entity
findings.source: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 Article 5(5), consolidated 10 January 2025
findings.talk_use: Q&A on tools built in a network: clinical use of a device needs this path or a CE mark.

findings.claim: The pending MDR/IVDR revision would move medical devices from Section A to Section B of AI Act Annex I, so that most AI Act duties would not apply to them directly; it is not adopted.
findings.detail: The first Council presidency compromise (31 August 2026) keeps the Commission's idea. In July 2026 Deutsches Ärzteblatt reported that the Parliament rapporteur expected trilogue at the end of 2026 or early 2027. Bitkom (October 2026) says Germany proposes in a non-paper at least class IIa for AI devices.
findings.quote: should therefore be moved from Section A to Section B
findings.source: Council of the EU, Presidency working document ST 12273/26
findings.talk_use: Q&A outlook: a definite answer on AI medical devices is not possible today.

findings.claim: The European Health Data Space regulation applies in general from 26 March 2027, and its rules on secondary use from 26 March 2029.
findings.detail: Article 105. Data holders must then make data from electronic health records available for secondary use (Article 51(1)(a)). Genomic, other omics, wellness and some further categories follow on 26 March 2031. National rules are part of the pending GeDIG bill. The German government says the EHDS opt-out does not extend to own-data research under draft section 24.
findings.quote: Chapter IV shall apply from 26 March 2029.
findings.source: Regulation (EU) 2025/327, Articles 51 and 105
findings.talk_use: Outlook slide: hospitals will have to make record data available from 2029, so structuring pays off.

findings.claim: A local LLM pipeline removed about 98% of identifying characters from 100 clinical letters, yet only 81 letters had no missed identifier.
findings.detail: LLM-Anonymizer with Llama-3 70B, Dresden, 2024 preprint. 1.95% of identifying characters were missed and 0.85% of characters wrongly redacted. The abstract of the later version, read on a third-party page, reports 250 letters, 99.24% removed and 2.43% over-redacted; its per-letter figure was not seen. High average recall does not mean every document is safe.
findings.number: 98.05% of characters; 81 letters without a miss
findings.quote: our system missed only 1.95% of personal identifying information
findings.source: Wiest et al., LLM-Anonymizer, medRxiv 2024 (later NEJM AI, not accessible)
findings.talk_use: Slide or Q&A: one number that shows why automatic de-identification is not anonymisation.

findings.claim: Language models fine-tuned on real hospital records can reproduce training content: a Yale study counted 3,192 regenerated pieces of protected health information among 10,000 training records.
findings.detail: Outputs for training records were screened by a detector and each hit was checked against the record. Memorisation ratios for 30 consecutive tokens ranged from 2% to 30%. Preprint version 3 read; a search snippet reports publication in Nature Communications 2026 (not read). Prompts came from training records, so this does not describe retrieval-only use.
findings.quote: regenerate 3,192 protected health information (PHI)
findings.source: Li et al., Memorization in Large Language Models in Medicine, arXiv 2509.08604v3
findings.talk_use: Q&A: why a fine-tuned model may itself be sensitive, while retrieval leaves data in a controlled store.

findings.claim: The Dutch data protection authority reported a data breach in which a GP practice employee entered patients' medical data into an AI chatbot against the practice's rules.
findings.detail: Official notice, page dated 6 August 2024. The authority calls sharing such data with a tech company a major privacy violation and says notification to the authority and the victims is often mandatory. No documented German hospital case was found in this search.
findings.quote: had een medewerker van een huisartsenpraktijk – tegen de afspraken in – medische gegevens van patiënten ingevoerd in een AI-chatbot
findings.source: Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens, notice on AI chatbots and data breaches
findings.talk_use: Q&A: a real case from a neighbour country; a safe internal tool removes the need for workarounds.

findings.claim: The German Medical Association says outside operators of AI systems must be bound to secrecy and that patients must be informed about the processing in plain language.
findings.detail: 2025 statement on AI in medicine. It refers to Articles 12 to 14 GDPR, asks for systematic evaluation before broad use and stresses that doctors need skills to check AI output. Professional guidance, not law.
findings.quote: dass diese zur Geheimhaltung zu verpflichten sind und sich die Schweigepflicht insoweit auch auf diese mitwirkenden Dienstleister erstreckt
findings.source: Bundesärztekammer, Von ärztlicher Kunst mit Künstlicher Intelligenz
findings.talk_use: Q&A: the profession's own position on AI vendors and patient information.

caveats: Background only, no legal advice; UKM data protection, IT security and the Ethik-Kommission Westfalen-Lippe decide concrete cases.

GDSG NW is repealed since 1 July 2025 although the research question still named it. A keyword search of KHGG NRW (version of 1 July 2025) found no general patient-data provision. That DSG NRW plus GDNG now fill the gap for UKM is an inference.
GeDIG, MDR/IVDR revision and the GDPR part of the Digital Omnibus are drafts. That they were not adopted by 22 November 2026 rests on searches, not on a full procedural check.
Whether fine-tuning a model counts as research under section 6 GDNG today is arguable; the draft calls its wording a clarification, the state authorities want clearer text.
CJEU SRB concerns Regulation 2018/1725 for EU bodies; applying it to GDPR cases is the common reading.
LLM-Anonymizer figures differ between preprint (100 letters, 98.05%) and later abstract (250 letters, 99.24%). Do not mix them.
AI Act Article 2 was read on a private mirror site because EUR-Lex delivered no text. German statutes are unofficial consolidated versions.
Sections 203 StGB and 393 SGB V are summarised; not every exception is listed.
gaps: No UKM or University of Münster rule on ChatGPT and patient data was found; check the intranet.
No DFG, Deutscher Ethikrat or BSI document was read.
No BfArM statement on LLM summarisers was found; Workum et al. (SSRN 2025) was not read.
Rules of the Ethik-Kommission Westfalen-Lippe for retrospective or anonymised data: the applicant guide of 31 March 2026 showed nothing on this in a keyword search.
In-house and Rule 11 changes in the MDR proposal were not verified in the primary text.
EDPB draft Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation were only seen through a law-firm article.
No documented German hospital incident with ChatGPT and patient data; the session's web search budget ran out before further searches.
